meta.scenario: techno 32-bar textural blend — same key, both tracks sparse breakdown, mid-range left fully open, atmospheric merge rather than functional swap
meta.source: Berghain Kantine — Surgeon b2b Paula Temple 2017

transition_arc: Both tracks share the same key (11A, B minor). T1 exits during a 32-bar atmospheric breakdown — the kick drops at bar 80 and the track becomes a wash of filtered noise and sub-pulsing. T2's intro is a 32-bar minimal sparse section: a very slow kick pattern with hi-hats and dark pads. Same key means mid-range content (the most identity-defining element of techno) can be left fully open (other:0.7) — no harmonic clash. The 32-bar window allows a genuinely atmospheric merge: the listener cannot tell when T1 stopped being the primary source and T2 took over. The bass swap fires at bar 16 of the 32-bar window. No mid suppression needed because same key means T2's dark pads complement T1's filter sweeps rather than clashing.

annotated_actions.t1_state: T1 bar 0: peak techno groove, kick+industrial noise+sub, RMS 0.65
T1 bar 72: 8 bars before T2 fade_in at bar 80. Groove still running but T1's breakdown is approaching, drums=0.50, rms=0.42
annotated_actions.why: Bass pre-cut 8 bars before T2 enters. The breakdown at bar 80 will naturally strip T1's sub — this eq enforces it from bar 72, giving 8 bars of clean sub absence before T2 arrives. In techno, an early bass cut is less noticeable than in house because the sub is often already being filtered by the producer in the last bars before a breakdown.
Kill T2 bass at fade start — prevents dual basslines during blend. EQ is persistent; will be restored at bass_swap point.

annotated_actions.t1_state: T1 bar 80: breakdown — kick drops out, filtered noise wash, drums=0.10, harmonic=0.15, rms=0.20
annotated_actions.t2_state: T2 bar 0: sparse intro, slow kick pattern, dark pads, drums=0.18, harmonic=0.12, rms=0.15
annotated_actions.why: 32-bar blend window — appropriate for this spare, atmospheric techno style. other:0.7 is safe and correct: same key (11A=11A) means T2's dark pad content is harmonically identical — layering at 0.7 creates the atmospheric merge rather than clash. drums:0.5 (not 0.8) — T2's intro kick is sparse and slow; introducing it at low volume first prevents a sudden kick-doubling on top of T1's breakdown. from_bar=0 — T2 starts from its actual first beat (no silence to skip). stems={drums:0.8, bass:0.0, other:0.6} — T2 enters with 80% drums, no bass (held for bass_swap), 60% atmosphere.

annotated_actions.t1_state: T1 bar 96: breakdown continues — sub absent, drums=0.08, harmonic=0.10, rms=0.12
annotated_actions.t2_state: T2 bar 16 (from_bar=0, 16 bars elapsed): sub-pulsing beginning, harmonic rising to 0.20
annotated_actions.why: Midpoint of the 32-bar window (80 + 16 = 96). T1's sub has been absent since bar 72. The swap releases T2's bass stem. In techno breakdowns, this is often the moment the new track's sub-pulse first becomes perceptible — the audience feels a shift in the sub register as T2's kick weight takes over. No drama, just a gradual handoff of the low-end anchor.
Restore T2 bass at bass_swap point — T1 bass is now HPF-cut, T2 bass can come in.

Simultaneous with T2 fade_in. 32-bar fade_out. T1's atmospheric breakdown content (filtered noise, pads) fades over 32 bars as T2's equivalent elements rise. At bar 96 (midpoint) both are equal — the mix is at maximum ambiguity, where neither track dominates. This is intentional in atmospheric techno transitions.

annotated_actions.t2_state: T2 bar 32: full techno groove arrives — kick+sub+industrial texture, RMS 0.62
annotated_actions.why: T2 full groove fires as T1 reaches zero. The 32-bar atmospheric merge complete. from_bar = fade_in.from_bar(0) + fade_in.duration_bars(32) = 32. T2's kick and sub arrive with impact precisely because 32 bars of sparse atmospheric content preceded them — dynamic contrast amplifies the drop.
